If the Hudsonian orogen is the product of plate tectonics then it is to be expect- ed that the bounding Archean cratons moved relative to one another, and these movements should be reflected in their paths of apparent polar move- ment. For example, if the Hudsonian orogen is the product of the Wilson cycle, that is, of an opening and closing ocean, then one possible paleomagnet- ic signature is a complimentary pair of pre-Hudsonian polar loops (each corresponding to movements of the bounding cratons during the opening and closing phases) which meet at their young end at the close of the Hudsonian orogeny, and which will come together, but not generally meet, at their old- er end (Fig. 2). Twenty-one samples from the Dogrib dykes have been dated by the whole- rock K/Ar method by Leech (1966) and gave ages ranging from 900 m.y. to 2310 m.y. From K/Ar studies, Fahrig and Wan- less (1963) suggested an age of about 2150 m.y. At sites 30NE and 33 the inclinations are lower. The approximate, but inexact, agreement between dykes and their contact rocks is a common effect, and is presumably caused by interaction between the fields of contact and diabase as they become magnetized at somewhat different times (Irving et al., 1972; Park, in press). At greater distances from the Indin dykes, notably in Dogrib diabase around Yellowknife, the directions are very different. Hence the contact test shows that the magnetization of the Indin dykes was probably acquired at the time of cooling. Any pervasive later magnetization event would also have remagne- tized the Dogrib diabase in the same direction, which it has not. They were collected in the first place Because it was felt that like the “X” dykes they could belong to the Dogrib swarm. The approximate, but inexact, agreement between dykes and their contact rocks is a common effect, and is presumably caused by interaction between the fields of contact and diabase as they become magnetized at somewhat different times (Irving et al., 1972; Park, in press). Indin diabase is massive, displays ophitic texture, and is composed of about equal amounts of plagioclase and pyroxene, with minor olivine, iron ores, and sphene. INTRODUCTION The cratonic regions of east-central Africa are partially overlain by Pre- cambrian sedimentary formations (Fig. 1) predominantly of elastic lithology, and which in several cases are partially incorporated into later mobile belts. Their maximum ages are loosely defined by age dates derived from basement rocks on which they lie, and minimum ages are sometimes available from igneous rocks intrusive into them. A summary of known age relationships of 136 Precambrian formations in central Africa based on information available to 1970 is given by Cahen (1970). It has already been suggested (McElhinny et al., 1968) that palaeomagnetism may provide a means of dating Precambrian formations whose ages cannot closely be defined by other means. Th

Identification of the loop in the a.p.w. curve between c. 630-450 m.y. is also supported by Cambrian to Ordovician poles from South America (Thompson, 1973) which when corrected for Phanerozoic drift define apparent polar movement closely comparable to that identified from African and other results. Palaeomagnetic evidence is consistent with sedimentation of the Plateau Series having continued to Early Palaeozoic times in the Lake Tanganyika region, and it may thus correlate in part with the Kundelungu System of Katanga and the Luapula Beds of the Zambia-Zaire border. The two signifi- cant sites from the southern outcrop however do not agree with VGPs obtain- ed from the Lake Tanganyika outcrop, and the better grouped of these (17) lies near the a.p.w. curve at 900-1000 m.y. It is also close to the pole from the Abercorn Sandstone and indeed the lithology (medium to coarse-grained sandstone) is more like that of the type Abercorn Sandstone than the fine- grained Plateau Series of sites l-14; however, as a single site only it is not possible to exclude correlation with the 630-450 m.y. loop as an alternative possibility. Mbala Dolerites, Zambia-Tanzania border The Abercorn Sandstone formation is extensively intruded by dolerite along the southeastern margin of Lake Tanganyika (Fig. 2A). Most of these intrusions are highly weathered and visible on the surface only as loose boulders. Of the two significant sites of this collection, site 36 is from a sill outcropping at Kalambo Falls on the Zambia-Tanzania border and site 39 is from an intrusion in the Lunzua valley south of Lake Tanganyika. These dolerites contain fresh plagioclase feldspar with pyroxene and titanomagnetite in an intersertal relationship. The pyroxene is uralitized to a variable degree and the titanomagnetite grains are marginally altered; they show a minor amount of subdivision by ilmenite lamellae. Intensities of magnetization are high (8 - 10-1-2 - 10B2 G) and only site 39 is significant before cleaning. With a.f. treatment magnetic moments of the samples with high initial values drop dramatically and are accompanied by large changes in direction (Fig. 5A). Secondly, these formations are mostly too late to be related to preceding erogenic episodes as molasse deposits, and indeed their characteristics are generally not commensurate with such an explanation. They contrast marked- ly with geosynclinal formations involved in the Kibaran-Irumide folding (1300-1100 m.y.) whose minimum ages are still currently only defined by intrusive igneous rocks. The line of the Kibaran belt in western Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda was the site of thick miogeosynclinal sedimen- tation prior to the tight folding of this belt at c. 1300, and the type Karagwe- Ankolean of Tanzania (Stockley and Williams, 1938) includes over 13,000 m of orthoquartzites and greywackes and may reach 20,000 m in Uganda. The Itiaso Group lying below the Bukoban system in west-central Tanzania and correlated with the Karagwe-Ankolean (Teale, 1931) exceeds 3000 m. Grey- wacke-type sedimentation had, however, largely terminated by the time the Bukoban System was deposited and only a few greywackes occur in the basal Masontwa Group (Halligan, 1962). In southern Tanzania the Ukinga Group (> 1300 m.y.) lying below the Buanji Series comprises over 3000 m of mio- 159 geosynclinal sediments (Harpum, 1955). It may postdate the Mbala dolerites since these are not found intruding it. Mbala Dolerites, Zambia-Tanzania border The Abercorn Sandstone formation is extensively intruded by dolerite along the southeastern margin of Lake Tanganyika (Fig. 2A). Most of these intrusions are highly weathered and visible on the surface only as loose boulders. Of the two significant sites of this collection, site 36 is from a sill outcropping at Kalambo Falls on the Zambia-Tanzania border and site 39 is from an intrusion in the Lunzua valley south of Lake Tanganyika. These dolerites contain fresh plagioclase feldspar with pyroxene and titanomagnetite in an intersertal relationship. The pyroxene is uralitized to a variable degree and the titanomagnetite grains are marginally altered; they show a minor amount of subdivision by ilmenite lamellae. The line of the Kibaran belt in western Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda was the site of thick miogeosynclinal sedimen- tation prior to the tight folding of this belt at c. 1300, and the type Karagwe- Ankolean of Tanzania (Stockley and Williams, 1938) includes over 13,000 m of orthoquartzites and greywackes and may reach 20,000 m in Uganda. The Itiaso Group lying below the Bukoban system in west-central Tanzania and correlated with the Karagwe-Ankolean (Teale, 1931) exceeds 3000 m. They contrast marked- ly with geosynclinal formations involved in the Kibaran-Irumide folding (1300-1100 m.y.) whose minimum ages are still currently only defined by intrusive igneous rocks. The line of the Kibaran belt in western Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda was the site of thick miogeosynclinal sedimen- tation prior to the tight folding of this belt at c. 1300, and the type Karagwe- Ankolean of Tanzania (Stockley and Williams, 1938) includes over 13,000 m of orthoquartzites and greywackes and may reach 20,000 m in Uganda. Grey- wacke-type sedimentation had, however, largely terminated by the time the Bukoban System was deposited and only a few greywackes occur in the basal Masontwa Group (Halligan, 1962). The main exposure is in the Twin Sisters Range (Fig. 1), where the dunite mass forms an elliptical outcrop pattern 16km long and an average of 5.5 km wide, elongate to the NNW. (Received November 4, 1971) This letter reports on paleomagnetic and rock magnetic studies of slightly serpenti- nized (0-15 vol.%) dunite from the Twin Sisters Range and Goat Mountain, north- western Washington State, U.S.A. The sample areas are restricted to the northwestern and southern margins of the dunite body, but results to date suggest that the remanent magnetism of little-altered dunite in the Twin Sisters Intrusion is stable against alter- nating field demagnetization and thermal magnetic cleaning, and that it converges to an esatward and down dipping direction with respect to geographic coordinates. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: NODIO- RITE, COCHISE COUNTY, ARIZONA' HENRY SPALL Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES), University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado 80302 ABSTRACT Block samples were collected in an east-west profile across the 1,655 m.y.-old Johnny Lyon granodiorite, Cochise County, Arizona. Progressive alternating field demagnetization shows that the NRM directions are stable to 175 Oe, and remain tightly grouped. Beyond this field the angular changes are large and irregular. The mean directions initially and after 175 Oe are remote from either the axial or the inclined present fields. The corresponding paleomagnetic pole after 175 Oe shows good agreement with poles from Cretaceous rocks from North America. This independent evidence supports the conclusion from isotopic studies (Silver and Deutsch 1963) that the granodiorite was profoundly affected by Cretaceous alteration processes. INTRODUCTION One of the objects in studying the natural remnant magnetization (NRM) of rocks is to determine dated paleomagnetic pole positions. For Precambrian rocks, strict criteria must be applied to ensure that the magnetization is both stable and reliable. Here the Cutler formation consists of massive sandstone interlayered with siltstone and occasional conglomeratic lenses. The sand- stone is reddish brown in color, medium-fine grained and well cemented. Although the Cutler formation has not been subdivided into members at this locality, it can be subdivided into 5 mem- bers a few kilometers to the west. These are the Halgaito shale (which interfingers with the Elephant Canyon formation), the Cedar Mesa sandstone, the Organ Rock shal

Toward the bottom of the section a massive tan colored sandstone was encountered that may be the equivalent of the Cedar Mesa sandstone member. The lowest stratigraphic in- terval is rather similar to the upper section and probably represents portions of the Halgaito shale member. The total thickness of the Cutler formation at this locality is about 200 meters and the beds dip 2 ø to the south. The uppermost shales sampled are probably equivalent to the shale overlying the White Rim sandstone that is believed to be of early Leonardtan age [Baars and Seaget, 1970]. Consequently the portion of the Cutler sampled in this study probably ranges from middle Wolfcampian to middle Leonardtan in age, a range encompassing most of the Lower Permian. The Cutler formation was first studied paleomagnetically by Graham [1955] in a sur- vey paper on Paleozoic and Mesozoic rocks from the western United States. More recently Fartel and May [1969] collected the entire Cutler formation in the Monument Valley area but had to reject 90% of their data because of magnetic instability. The hematite grains usually contain magnetite relics (martire). Whether this reflects a highly oxidized source material or whether the hematite formed from magnetite during subsequent diagenesis cannot. be decided. In recent years several authors have called attention to the possibility of using magnetic reversals as a tool for stratigraphic correlation [Picard, 1964; Burek, 1967, 1970; McMahon and Strangway, 1968a, b; Helsley, 1969]. Before this can be done successfully on a world- wide scale a standard section must be estab- lished. This requires dense stratigraphic sam- pling where the spacing depends on parameters such as rate of deposition and continuity of the section. For example, the lowest normal interval in the Moenkopi formation extends stratigraphi- cally over 18 meters at Gateway, Colorado, and thins to only 3 meters in Monument Valley, Arizona [Helsley, 1969]. The thinning can be explained by a decrease in the sedimentation rate away from the source area. Before this can be done successfully on a world- wide scale a standard section must be estab- lished. This requires dense stratigraphic sam- pling where the spacing depends on parameters such as rate of deposition and continuity of the section. The thinning can be explained by a decrease in the sedimentation rate away from the source area. Cornwell* (Received 1966 May 9) Summary The directions of magnetization and the magnetic properties of the Exeter lavas and the associated red sediments have been measured. The lavas have been placed in the Stephanian on the basis of recent age deter- minations (280 m.y.) but they are interbedded with the desert type sedi- ments typical of New Red Sandstone times in southwest England. The directions of the lavas generally show little scatter and are very resistant to both thermal and a.c. demagnetization. This is probably connected with the fact that their remanence is to a large extent due to haematite and a crystallization remanence (CRM). It is likely that the CRM was formed when the lavas were exposed to weathering soon after they were extruded in desert conditions. The palaeomagnetic pole position agrees with that established by an earlier investigation of the lavas. The associated sedi- ments are not altogether satisfactory for rock magnetic studies owing to their friable nature but yield a pole position similar to that of the lavas. 1. Mussett and R. L. Hay (Received 1970 April 6) Summary Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) has been measured in 21 lava flows and 1 tuff in the south-west wall of Ngorongoro caldera, Tanzania. The lowest three lavas are normally magnetized, the next two have inter- mediate directions, and the remainder are reversed ; potassium-argon dating places the reversal at 2.45 My, corresponding to the Gauss- Matuyama epoch boundary. Alternating-field demagnetization was effective in removing the ubiquitous lightning-produced secondary magnetizations, but partial thermal demagnetization was not. Curie temperatures of the lavas fell into two groups: 250"-350°C and 570"- 585 "C, probably corresponding to unoxidized and oxidized titanomagne- tites respectively. NRM directions in the lavas occurred in several distinct and stratigraphically continuous groups, suggesting intermittent eruption of groups of lavas. No correspondence was found between NRM groups and other parameters, such as Curie temperatures. The dispersion of mean NRM directions is large in comparison with late Quaternary lavas from l

ie temperatures. The dispersion of mean NRM directions is large in comparison with late Quaternary lavas from low latitudes in the Pacific basin, but probably is not large relative to the proportion of the geomagnetic field in Africa that is non-dipolar. The mean palaeomagnetic pole is offset 10.5" from the geographic pole, but because of the large dispersion, the difference is not considered significant. Upon thermal demagnetization, a stable primary component of magnetization could be isolated in most of the samples. Geology The Lamotte formation crops out only in the St Francois Mountains region of South-eastern Missouri. Radioactive dating of the Precambrian igneous rocks of St Francois Mountains has been performed by Adams (1959), Allen et al. (1960), and Tilton, Weatherill & Davis (1962). Geology The Lamotte formation crops out only in the St Francois Mountains region of South-eastern Missouri. Geology The Lamotte formation crops out only in the St Francois Mountains region of South-eastern Missouri. The formation is a white sandstone and has been shown to be of Upper Cambrian age, approximately 500My old, primarily because of its unconformable relationship with the Precambrian rocks and its conformable and gradational contact with the overlying Bonne Terre dolomite (Ojakangas 1960). Strickland and Hale pegma- tites were chosen because they belong to a relatively small group of pegmatites with measurable remanent magnetization. Ilmenomagnetite occurs in the contact zone of the Strickland pegmatite and hematite is found dispersed throughout the Hale pegmatite. The sense of the displacement of the Pliocene pole position suggests that the col- lection site may have undergone a clockwise rotation of about 30 ° since the rocks were magnetized. If this is the case it suggests that portions of western North America have rotated as independent blocks in addition to the lateral translations typical of sea-floor spreading models. 1. Introduction In a study of modern red sediments and the way in which they become magnetized, it has been pos- sible to determine a Pliocene paleomagnetic pole position from Baja California, Mexico. The olivine in the Coro- nation Sills is largely altered to lamellar minerals with high birefringence that range in color from golden yellow to pale green. The sills were sampled west of Copper- mine River where they form prominent cuesta ridges, ideal for collecting oriented cores by rock drill. The objects of this study are therefore three fold: firstly to obtain chemical, petrographic and paleomagnetic data from the Coronation Sills; secondly to derive a pole position for them from stability tested data, and to combine the results with those of Fahrig et al. (1971 ) to update the Franklin Magnetic Interval Pole; and thirdly to use the Coronation Sills to com- pare the various factors that make up the sta- bility spectra of these tholeiitic sheets. These factors may be usefully extrapolated to similar sheets that occur at many critical horizons in the geological column. Samples were partially demagnetized by both ac and thermal techniques. Magnetic directions were essentially the same regardless of treat- ment. Polished section and Curie temperature analysis indicate that the principal magnetic phase is low-titanium titanomagnetite. In many samples, titanomagnetite is the only magnetic iron oxide; in some samples, hematite occurs additionally. However, those samples contain- ing hematite show the same remanent direc- tions as those containing only titanomagnetite. All of our studies indicate that the magnetiza- tion is thermoremanent magnetization (TRM) acquired during the Cambrian and Ordovician. Our results suggest that either little polar wandering occurred between the early and late Paleozoic or, if substantial wandering did oc- cur, by late Paleozoic time the paleopole

fter deposition (DRM), (2) later, perhaps much later, by chemical altera- tion of iron oxides or iron silicates (CRM), or (3) later, by heating of the magnetic oxides (PTRM). As one might expect and as is evident from Figure 6, there is a great deal of scatter in the results from any one period. The fact that some of the lower Paleozoic paleopoles lie close to those obtained from upper Paleozoic rocks has been used by some (Irving, 1964; Creer, 1968) to indicate that those particular rocks were largely remagnetized during the late Paleozoic. Thermoremanent magnetization (TRM), ac- quired by an igneous rock body as it cools through a range of blocking temperatures, is generally more reliable in determination of a paleopole position. The rock can be accurately dated radiometrically; the initial magnetization was acquired essentially at one moment and is commonly stable; later diagenetic changes oc- cur less readily in igneous rocks (particularly intrusives) than they do in sediments. What is needed in paleomagnetic studies of the lower Paleozoic are more data from igneous rocks. In this note we report paleomagnetic data ob- tained from intrusive igneous rocks in Colorado which have been dated as lower Paleozoic by isotopic methods. Washington 99004 Anomalous Paleomagnetic Pole from Isotopically Dated Cambro-Ordovician Intrusives in Colorado ABSTRACT Paleomagnetic data from isotopically dated Cambrian and Ordovician plutons in central Colorado indicate a Cambrian-Ordovician paleopole close to the late Paleozoic pole posi- tion. Samples were partially demagnetized by both ac and thermal techniques. Magnetic directions were essentially the same regardless of treat- ment. Polished section and Curie temperature analysis indicate that the principal magnetic phase is low-titanium titanomagnetite. In many samples, titanomagnetite is the only magnetic iron oxide; in some samples, hematite occurs additionally. However, those samples contain- ing hematite show the same remanent direc- tions as those containing only titanomagnetite. All of our studies indicate that the magnetiza- tion is thermoremanent magnetization (TRM) acquired during the Cambrian and Ordovician. Our results suggest that either little polar wandering occurred between the early and late Paleozoic or, if substantial wandering did oc- cur, by late Paleozoic time the paleopole has returned to a position that was nearly coinci- dent with that of the early Paleozoic. statistically significant data were obtained from the eight basalt samples despite alternating field (AF) demagnetization up to 700 oe. 2. Magnetic vectors of the seven Mdrida redbed samples after thermal demagnetization to 550°C (D = 358, I ^ -|~ 10' l( = 6) resemble the present mag­ netic field, suggesting Quaternary-Holocene acquisi­ tion of remanence. 3. Twenty-two redbed samples from the Sabaneta facies, after thermal demagnetization to 550°C, give moderately consistent paleomagnetic vectors (D = 223, I = -j- 15, k = 11), which are best interpreted as of secondary origin acquired after Late Permian folding. If this secondary remanence is considered to be Late Permian, it implies a post-Permian 60° clockwise rota­ tion of the Venezuelan Andes for which there is no corroborating paleomagnetic or tectonic evidence. Dis­ regarding polarity, the Sabaneta magnetic axis closely resembles that for the La Quinta Formation in the type area which was acquired during Tertiary Andean up­ lift. It is concluded that the Sabaneta remanence was acquired contemporaneously in Tertiary time. Similarly, the northeast-southwest declination is anomalous and a clockwise tectonic rotation within the Venezuelan Andes is suggested in possible explanation. •Manuscript received, March 2, 197

INTRODUCTION One of the major unconformities in the Ven­ ezuelan Andes separates Mesozoic formations from the underlying late Paleozoic section. Re­ cently we (Hargraves and Shagam, 1969) re­ ported on the paleomagnetic characters of the La Quinta Formation, the basal unit of the sec­ tion above the unconformity. The Sabaneta and Merida facies, subjects of this paleomagnetic study, lie below the unconformity in association with Permo-Carboniferous marine shale and limestone. The natural remanent magnetism (NRM) of the La Quinta rocks was concluded to be of secondary origin, acquired during The Tertiary uplift of the Andes. The relatively drab, grayish-red color of most specimens appears to be related in part to red-stained matrix and in part to reddish-brown weathered clastic feldspar grains, being lighter in tone in those specimens with little matrix. The vesicular basalt specimens (locality 2A) were collected from a dike 2 m wide intruded into the Sabaneta facies. The volcanic rocks also are present as a few scattered, thin lava flows in the formation. In thin section these specimens display a sub-ophitic texture, but the most notable feature from a paleomagnetic point of view is the fact that augite is largely altered to amphibole or chlorite and plagioclase is markedly turbid. These effects are believed related to deuteric alteration. Depositional Environment We agree in general with the views of Ar­ nold (1966, p. 2373) concerning the deposi­ tional environments of the Merida and Sa­ baneta facies. AGE OF MAGNETISM The Sabaneta redbeds were folded tightly in pre-La Quinta time, probably in Middle to Late Permian. Subsequently, together with the La Quinta Formation, the older redbeds were sub­ ject to early Tertiary and later pulses of uplift. It is possible that the acquisition of the sec­ ondary remanence was associated with the Late Permian diastrophism. Japan (43.3N, 145.8E). Direction of magnetization of samples from the marginal parts of some monzonite or piclitic dolerite complex are quite dif- ferent from those from the central parts. This suggests that the transitional change of geomagnetic field polarity might have occurred during cooling of the rock body. The paleomagnetic results suggest the presence of two short reversed zones in the Upper Cretaceous in which normal polarity was predo- minant. Recent K-A age determinations suggest that these reversals took place at 88 m.y. and 84 m.y. ago. They should become important time markers in Cretaceous paleomagnetic stratigraphy. 1. Japan. Due to the remarkable differentiated rock facies, from porphyritic basalt to monzonite, and their peculiar chemical composition, they were the subject of many petrographic studies (SUZUKI, 1938; MAGI, 1958, 1968, etc.). We re- ported the paleomagnetic results of these rocks (FUJIWARA and NAGASE, 1965). Since then, further field and laboratory works and recent K-A age determina- tions have brought up some new aspects in terms of the age and activity of al- kaline rocks in the Nemuro Peninsula. Recently Northcote (1969) published the results of detailed geologic mapping, petrologic investigations, and K-Ar dating of the various intrusive phases of the entire batholith. The batholith is unconformably overlain by Lower Jurassic sediments (upper Hettangian and Sine- murian-Frebold and Tipper 1969) containing clasts from the batholith and by younger rocks. Stratigraphically, therefore, the batholith was emplaced during the Late Triassic (upper Norian or Rhaetian) and /or Lower Jurassic (lower Hettangian) and it was immediately unroofed. The intruded Nicola Group has been contact metamorphosed to hornfels, but it does not ap- pear to have been regionally metamorphosed. Baadsgaard et al. (1961) determined a radio- metric age of 186 f 9 m.y. for the batholith using the K-Ar method on biotite. Dirom (1965) (in White et al. 1967) obtained a concordant average age of 200 f 8 m.y. on eight samples from the batholith using the K-Ar method on biotite and hornblende excluding one porphyry sample which gave 171 + 12 m.y. for which a second sample gave 199 f 8 m.y. White et al. (1967) reported 26 K-Ar dates on biotites from all 7 intrusive phases of the batholith. They obtained an average of 198 f 8 m.y. and were not able to distinguish between the phase ages. The major phases are concentrically arranged (Fig. 1) progressing from the older marginal mesozonal phases (I) and (2) through phases of intermediate age (3), (4), and (5) to the younger epizonal phases (6) and (7) of the core. In general, the mean percentages of magnetite and mafic min- erals and the mean specific gravity decreases progressively from the oldest (1) to youngest (7) phase while the mean percentages of quartz and orthoclase tend to increase. The lack of chilled contacts between phases indicates that they cooled nearly simultaneously. Preservation of the original textures and structures indicates that the batholith has not been metamorphosed since emplacement. Foliation decreases in intensity from moderate in the marginal phases to slight in the core phases. In general, the foliation strikes parallel to and dips toward the margins of the batholith. basic magma with the ore representing the terminal cooling stage. In the light of present knowledge, therefore, it appears that the Guichon Batholith was em- placed during the Late Triassic about 198 + 8 m.y. ago; all intrusive phases cooled essentially contemporaneously; the batholith was unroofed and being eroded by Early Jurassic; and, it has not beenmetamorphosed since emplacement. Sampling and Measurement Ninety-two (92) cores, oriented in situ by sun compass, were collected from 19 sites on the batholith (Fig. 1) with the majority of sites representing the Hybrid (1) and Highland Valley (2) phases because of their higher magnetite con- tent. Two specimens were cut from each core and their natural remanent magnetizations (n.r.m.) measured using methods described by Larochelle and Christie (1967). One pilot specimen from each site was demagnetized (Larochelle and Black 1965) stepwise in alternating field (a.f.) peak intensities of 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 650, afid 800 Oe with its remanence remeasured after each step. Definition of the Logan Loop More than 10 years ago DuBois discovered that paleomagnetic poles from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield formed a great loop (DuBois 1962, p. 69), which (on the present geographic grid) swept north from the equator at 150" W longitude up into North America, thence west and south to the equator at 170' E longitude. At that time, however, the apex of the loop was poorly defined, and it was not clear how much of the movement could be attributed to secondary components in some of the rock formations. Also, although he knew in general the sequence of events, the absolute ages of the origin of most of his formations were not known, so that it was impossible to estimate the rate at which this movement took place. Five relatively well-dated pole positions from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield (Table 6) define critical points on the polar wandering loop. As the apex of the loop is anchored by poles derived from the Logan sills and Logan dikes, we propose that this major polar wandering movement in Neohelikian2 time relative to the central Canadian Shield be called the Logan Loop. The Logan Loop indicates that continental drift and/or polar wandering took place in Neo- helikian time unless the earth's field had quite a different configuration from that of today. The rapid polar shift indicated by the Logan Loop occupied the same period of time as the Grenvillian orogeny. If orogenies generally reflect ocean-floor spreading and continental drift (Irving and Robertson 1969), then a period of rapid apparent polar wandering, expressing continental drift, would be expected to coincide with orogenic episodes. It is suggested then, that the Logan Loop and the Grenvillian orogeny are genetically related. The Grenville orogenic belt has been traced through western Scotland and Scandinavia (DuToit 1937), and it has been suggested that at that time, before the birth of the Atlantic, the Baltic and Canadian Shields were united. If so they should have moved as a single unit, and a paleomagnetic study of rocks of this age from the Baltic Shield should yield a polar loop similar to the Logan Loop (Fahrig et al. 1971). Definition of the Logan Loop More than 10 years ago DuBois discovered that paleomagnetic poles from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield formed a great loop (DuBois 1962, p. 69), which (on the present geographic grid) swept north from the equator at 150" W longitude up into North America, thence west and south to the equator at 170' E longitude. At that time, however, the apex of the loop was poorly defined, and it was not clear how much of the movement could be attributed to secondary components in some of the rock formations. Also, although he knew in general the sequence of events, the absolute ages of the origin of most of his formations were not known, so that it was impossible to estimate the rate at which this movement took place. Five relatively well-dated pole positions from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield (Table 6) define critical points on the polar wandering loop. As the apex of the loop is anchored by poles derived from the Logan sills and Logan dikes, we propose that this major polar wandering movement in Neohelikian2 time relative to the central Canadian Shield be called the Logan Loop. The Logan Loop indicates that continental drift and/or polar wandering took place in Neo- helikian time unless the earth's field had quite a different configuration from that of today. The rapid polar shift indicated by the Logan Loop occupied the same period of time as the Grenvillian orogeny. If orogenies generally reflect ocean-floor spreading and continental drift (Irving and Robertson 1969), then a period of rapid apparent polar wandering, expressing continental drift, would be expected to coincide with orogenic episodes. It is suggested then, that the Logan Loop and the Grenvillian orogeny are genetically related. The Grenville orogenic belt has been traced through western Scotland and Scandinavia (DuToit 1937), and it has been suggested that at that time, before the birth of the Atlantic, the Baltic and Canadian Shields were united. If so they should have moved as a single unit, and a paleomagnetic study of rocks of this age from the Baltic Shield should yield a polar loop similar to the Logan Loop (Fahrig et al. 1971). Definition of the Logan Loop More than 10 years ago DuBois discovered that paleomagnetic poles from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield formed a great loop (DuBois 1962, p. 69), which (on the present geographic grid) swept north from the equator at 150" W longitude up into North America, thence west and south to the equator at 170' E longitude. At that time, however, the apex of the loop was poorly defined, and it was not clear how much of the movement could be attributed to secondary components in some of the rock formations. Also, although he knew in general the sequence of events, the absolute ages of the origin of most of his formations were not known, so that it was impossible to estimate the rate at which this movement took place. Five relatively well-dated pole positions from late Proterozoic rocks of the Canadian Shield (Table 6) define critical points on the polar wandering loop. As the apex of the loop is anchored by poles derived from the Logan sills and Logan dikes, we propose that this major polar wandering movement in Neohelikian2 time relative to the central Canadian Shield be called the Logan Loop. They indicate a minimum apparent age of intrusion at 1880 m.y. This is older than published whole-rock ages from the same dikes, but is consistent with whole-rock ages of up to 2060 m.y. from other dikes in this area. The within-dike dispersion of the direc- tions of natural remanent magnetization de- creases during alternating field demagnetiza- tion up to 1400 oe. Thermal demagnetization, however, is not effective in removing second- ary magnetizations. After structural correction according to overlying Cambrian sediments, an over-all mean paleomagnetic pole from four dikes is obtained at 121° W., 43° N., which is in agreement with poles from Canadian Shield rocks of similar age. There is evidence in two of the dikes for a remagnetization episode, and the equivalent pole positions suggest that this may have occurred at the time of deposition of the Cambrian Flathead Sandstone. This study is concerned with some mafic dikes which intrude the core of the south- ern part of the Wind River Range. By isotopi- cally dating these rocks, it was intended to compare a paleomagnetic result from mafic dikes in the American Shield with determina- tions from dated mafic dike swarms in the Canadian Shield (for example, Fahrig and oth- ers, 1965). GEOLOGIC SETTING The Wind River Range is a northwest-trend- ing belt of high mountains, more than 100 mi long, which exposes crystalline Precambrian rocks. In the northwest sector of the Range, these are principally gray, lit-par-lit gneisses, ex- tensively cut by quartz, pegmatite, and granitic rocks (Richmond, 1945; Baker, 1946). At the southern end, schists predominate and are in- truded by granodiorite-quartz monzonite (Branson and Branson, 1941; Oftedahl, 1953; Parker, 1962; Hodge an

ntrusion. Petrographic evidence and the variation between sample splits suggest that alteration is the most critical factor in causing the large range in observed ages from these dikes. The highest pyroxene age is 1880 m.y.; the highest whole-rock age is 2060 m.y. Because of alteration this would give a minimum estimate of the apparent age of 1880 to 2060 m.y. for these southern Wind River dikes. EXPERIMENTAL METHODS The direction and moment of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of all the specimens were measured on a PAR spinner magnetometer, Model SM-1. One specimen from each sample was subjected to progressive alternating field (AF) demagnetization in fields of 175, 350, 700 and 1400 oe. A second speci- men from each sample was thermally demag- netized by the stepwise method in a field free space (+ 10 gamma) to 200, 300, 400, 500 and 570°C stages and the NRM was measured after the specimen had been cooled to labora- tory temperatures. All the demagnetization equipment is located in a shielded room (with a residual field of 200 gamma) and is described by Helsley (1969). In the early part of the work, an AF stage at 88 oe was also used, but with the exception of dike 5, there was little change in the NRM direction, and so this stage was omitted from subsequent studies. INTRODUCTION Within Mexico, volcanic lavas and pyroclas- tics cover more than one-third of the total land area. The two principal volcanic regions are the Cordilleran Province, and the Rio Lerma Prov- ince. The former extends from the United States-Mexico border to south of Guadalajara, and from the Pacific coast to Torreon in the Central Plateau. It is dominated by vast ignim- brite sheets. The Rio Lerma Province extends south and east of Guadalajara, and is sometimes called the Cent

hed. In common with other volcanic regions, stratigraphic studies in central Mexico are handicapped by the general lack of distinctive fossiliferous sedimentary horizons. he Rio Grande de Santiago Volcanics, Central Mexico ABSTRACT Seventy-two oriented cores of 2.5 cm diame- ter have been drilled from seven bodies com- prising part of a sequence of ignimbrite sheets interdigitated with basalts and basaltic ande- sites, in the Grand Canyon of the Rio Grande de Santiago of the Mexican Cordilleran Vol- canic Province. Field observations and whole- rock analyses reveal two groups: an olivine basalt-high alumina basalt-basaltic andesite se- ries, and a sequence of rhyolitic ignimbrite sheets, with some rhyolitic and obsidian lava flows. Crystal separation, partial melting of oceanic tholeiite, and simple mixing of basalt and oceanic sediments or granodiorite cannot acceptably explain the observed fractionation trends. The favored origin is a partial melting of a second or third stage product, such as a basalt or amphibolite enriched in K, Rb, Th, and Pb, relative to oceanic tholeiite. The ob- served fractionation trends are parallel to those of the andesite-dacites of the Mexico City re- gion, but the Rio Grande de Santiago rocks have a systematically higher K2O/SiC>2 ratio, which can be explained by a greater magma generation depth. stage product, such as a basalt or amphibolite enriched in K, Rb, Th, and Pb, relative to oceanic tholeiite. The ob- served fractionation trends are parallel to those of the andesite-dacites of the Mexico City re- gion, but the Rio Grande de Santiago rocks have a systematically higher K2O/SiC>2 ratio, which can be explained by a greater magma generation depth. The paleomagnetic polarity sequence with decreasing age is R,R,N,R,R,N,N, providing easily measurable markers of high potential stratigraphic value. The mean virtual geomag- netic pole is not significantly different from the present spin axis. The potassium-argon analyses show that the sampled section contains two dis- tinct volcanic episodes, from approximately t = 4.6 to 5.5. m.y. and from approximately t = 8.7 to 9-5 m.y. The polarities recorded by the youngest volcanic cycle are consistent with the predicted polarity time scale of Heirtzler and others (1968), while the older cycle polarities can be explained by minor modification of the predicted polarity scale, to include a short period of reversed polarity between 9.0 and 9.5 m.y., within the normal polarity anomaly 5 (t = 8.79 to 9.94 m.y.) of the time scale. The average Koenigsberger ratio is about 10. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: The Paleomagnetism of Diabase Dikes from the Grenville Province G. S. MURTHY~ Department of Physics, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta Received February 8, 1971 Revision accepted for publication April 8, 1971 A paleomagnetic study was attempted of the diabase dike swarm intruding the Grenville structural province of the Canadian Shield. Both the alternating field and thermal demagnetization studies indicated that the dikes have varying degrees of stability of magnetization. Some dikes were shown to have stable primary component of magnetization. Microscopic observations indicated that, in most cases, the primary magnetic mineral titanomagnetite was altered to titanomaghemite, probably due to low temperature oxidation. A good correlation is obtained between magnetic stability and relative abundance of titanomagnetite to titanomaghemite in that dike. The mean paleomagnetic pole for the Grenville dike swarm, which is probably of late Precambrian age, was computed to lie at 3.0 O N, 29.0 " W with Ags = 11.0 ". Comparison of this result with other Precambrian pole positions of similar age relative to North America suggests that the dikes were intruded after the Grenville orogeny. The Orkneys are nearly exclusively built up of flagstones and sandstones belonging to the Middle and Upper divisions of the Old Red Sandstone, the total stratigraphic thickness spanning about 5000 m. The geological structure of the islands is fairly simple. A thin volcanic zone consisting of at least two lava flows is found in the upper section of the Middle Old Red beds of East Mainland, Shapinsay and the Black Holm of Copinsay. The lava flows are dark green, highly decomposed basic rocks which are in part vesicular and contain pipe amygdales. Did the Southern Alps once form part of the drifting African continent, as has tentatively been suggested by Van Hilten and Zijderveld (1966)? Or did they just drift, or maybe only rotate individually as a Tectonophysics, 10 (1970) 639-661 639 Tectonophysics, 10 (1970) 639-661 smaller tectonic unit, as a result of movements in the Tethys zone? This paper presents new data from the same formation (Bolzano Quartz Porphyr~es) which Van Hilten studied (Leo), but now on the basis of a recent geologic and petrographic study by one of us (M.N.) and a col- lection of 206 samples. Finally, we will undertake a renewed comparison between the increasing number of paleomagnetic directions derived from Permian rocks from the extra-Alpine areas in Europe, the African Shield and from the Southern 41ps, in order to establish some reasonable limits to the wide range of suggestions and interpretations. GWLOGY OF THE BOLZANO QUARTZ PORPHYRIES After the Hercynian orogeny and subsequent peneplenization, a thick sequence of predominantly ignimbritic flows (rhyodacites and rhyolites) was deposited over a large area in the Southern Alps (Fig-l). Marmoiada, 1970 and Feltre, 1970). For the paleomagnetic investigation samples were collected from ten flows and two tuff layers (46 sites), The sampling site distribution is shown in the geological sketch map of Fig.1. On top of the volcanic series follow Upper Permian sandstones (GrtMener s.s.), the Upper Permian evaporites and limestones and finally the Triassic sequence. The whole sequence has remained fairly undisturbed, with minor faulting and moderate dips. In the course of our collection of the oriented hand samples, special care was taken in the determination of the tectonic strike and dip of the flows, thus restricting the sampling to tectonically unambiguous sites. To fit in the available paleomagnetic data, a position of Africa is required somewhere in the (present) Indian Ocean with respect to Eurasia, followed by a translation, with a counterclockwise rotation of about 40° in Late Mesozoic and Tertiary times. The arguments of Van Hilten (1964) are based upon the combined two Permian pole positions for Africa (which indeed, as has just been mentioned, do not agree with the Bullard reconstruction) and are also based upon an assumed ancient dextral character of many strike-slip faults in the Tethys shear zone: the peri-Adriatic fault in Italy (De Jong, 1967a), faults in Jugoslavia, the north Anatolian fault zone in Turkey etc. Some of these faults are still active at present (Ritsema, 1969). Volcanic rocks of Late Mesozoic age, i.e., Rajmahal traps and associated dykes and sills, are the oldest and possibly the only igneous rocks in the mainly sedimentary Gondwana sequence (Late Carboniferous to Middle Cretaceous) on the Indian subcontinent.
